Bloody Mary Confusion. A frequent conflation mistakes Mary I of England with Mary, Queen of Scots, using "Bloody Mary" to refer to both indiscriminately. These are distinct historical figures. Mary I ruled England from 1553 to 1558 and earned the "Bloody Mary" epithet for Protestant persecutions. Mary, Queen of Scots was a separate figure who ruled Scotland and was executed in England decades later. Confusion arises because both were queens named Mary and lived during the same tumultuous era.

Mary I of England, also called Bloody Mary, was the Catholic daughter of Henry VIII who ruled England and attempted to restore Catholicism after Edward VI's Protestant reign. She lived from 1516 to 1558. Mary, Queen of Scots lived from 1542 to 1587. She was the Catholic queen of Scotland who had claims to the English throne. She fled Scotland, was imprisoned in England, and was executed by her cousin Elizabeth I.

Mary I earned the "Bloody Mary" nickname for the execution of approximately three hundred Protestants during her reign, aimed at Catholic restoration but resulting in Protestant backlash and her enduring negative legacy. Mary, Queen of Scots played a different tragic role. Her imprisonment and execution became a symbol of Catholic martyrdom, and she had no part in Mary I's persecutions.

Mary I died in 1558 and was never called "Bloody Mary" in her own time. The epithet emerged after her death and solidified through later Protestant historians' writings. The two Marys were cousins and lived overlapping lifespans, but Mary I never ruled Scotland, and Mary of Scots never ruled England, though both had claims and ambitions tied to both realms.
